name: MemWeaver

paper.title: MemWeaver: A Hierarchical Memory from Textual Interactive Behaviors for Personalized Generation

construction.unit: a user's past document (behavior) as a graph node, plus one LLM-written user summary
construction.kept_as: past documents verbatim (truncated to fit the prompt); summary written by the LLM
construction.processing: embed each document (BGE-M3), K-means over the embeddings, link consecutive documents (temporal) and same-cluster documents (semantic); LLM summarizes each cluster, then merges the local summaries into one global summary
construction.writer: backbone LLM (Qwen3-8B or Llama-3.1-8B) for summaries; BGE-M3 for embeddings

organization.structure: per-user graph over the history (temporal chain + intra-cluster semantic edges) and one global preference summary
organization.stores: behavior graph (rebuilt per query in the code); cognitive memory text per user

management.operations: paper: incremental update links new documents to the last node, clusters the new batch on its own, and re-merges old and new local summaries; not in the released code

retrieval.candidates: random walk over the graph from the history item most similar to the query, at most 10 unique nodes (paper)
retrieval.selection: code: walked nodes reranked by BGE-M3 similarity, top 5 kept, topped up from the rest of the history if fewer
retrieval.budget: 5 past items plus the summary, input capped at 3000 tokens

use.context: 'User summary: ...' followed by the retrieved past items, the task instruction and the query

classify.note: The walk produces the candidates; the released code then keeps the 5 most similar by dense score. The summary sits beside the graph and is always included.

stages.ingestion: The input is a user's time-ordered list of past documents (e.g. paper titles and abstracts, reviews, headlines) from the LaMP profiles.
stages.construction: Each document is embedded with BGE-M3 and clustered with K-means (K = 5 in the paper); a graph links consecutive documents (temporal edges) and documents in the same cluster (semantic edges).
stages.organization: Two memories: the behavior graph over raw documents and a cognitive memory, a short text built by summarizing groups of documents and then merging those summaries (paper: time phases; code: K-means clusters).
stages.update: The paper describes incremental updates (append and link new documents, cluster the new batch alone, re-merge summaries), which track a full rebuild at lower cost in a simulation (Fig. 5); the released code rebuilds instead.
stages.retrieval: A random walk starts at the document most similar to the query and moves to neighbours with probability tied to query similarity, time gap and recency (alpha 1.5, lambda1 0.01, lambda2 0.02), for at most 10 steps; the code reranks the visited documents and keeps 5.
stages.answer: The LLM is prompted with the user summary, the selected past documents and the task query.
stages.learning: Training-free; ROPG and CFRAG baselines are trained on the LaMP training split, MemWeaver only uses the test split.

summary: Personalized generation from a user's past texts: the history becomes a graph (temporal and same-cluster semantic edges) that is sampled by a query-guided random walk, plus a two-stage LLM summary of the user's preferences, and both go into the prompt.

abstract.text: MemWeaver personalizes LLM outputs from the texts a user has written or interacted with. It keeps two memories: a behavioral memory, sampled per query by a random walk over a graph whose edges join time-adjacent and topically similar past documents, and a cognitive memory, an LLM summary of the user's preferences built from summaries of parts of the history. Both are placed in the prompt of an 8B model. On six LaMP tasks it beats plain retrievers and trained personalization retrievers (ROPG, CFRAG) on every metric.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.

headline: The answer model reads 5 raw past documents plus one LLM-written user summary; the graph only decides which 5.
In the released code the walked documents are reranked by dense similarity, so the walk acts as a candidate filter before plain dense top-5.
The paper builds the summary from time phases; the code (and App. D.1) builds it from K-means clusters.

discussion.takeaway: Choosing past documents by a walk that mixes query similarity with time structure, and adding an LLM summary of the user, beat plain and trained retrievers on all six LaMP tasks with 8B models; the concrete documents matter more than the summary.

claims.claim: MemWeaver is best on all twelve LaMP metrics with both backbones.
claims.evidence: Qwen3-8B LaMP-1 Acc 0.6733 vs 0.6566 (CFRAG), LaMP-3 MAE 0.2800 vs 0.3266, LaMP-5 R-1 0.4757 vs 0.4698; t-test p < 0.05. Table 1, §4.2

claims.claim: Both memories are needed, with behavioral memory as the base.
claims.evidence: Without behavioral memory LaMP-4 R-1 falls from 0.1724 to 0.1069; without cognitive memory to 0.1651. Table 2, §4.3.1

claims.claim: Edge weighting and semantic edges matter more than temporal edges, although temporal edges are traversed more.
claims.evidence: w/o edge weighting LaMP-1 0.5708, w/o semantic 0.6324, w/o temporal 0.6233 (full 0.6733); temporal edges are the majority of traversals on every task. Table 2, Fig. 3

claims.claim: Incremental updates approach a full rebuild at a fraction of the cost.
claims.evidence: Fig. 5 (accuracy and tasks/s vs history share); no table of numbers.
LaMP-1 Acc 0.673 vs 0.652 (Mem0), 0.650 (MemoRAG), 0.579 (Memory-R1). Table 5, App. C.2

limits: The paper has no limitations section; §4.6 notes that the best recency and continuity weights depend on the task.
reading: The prompt holds 5 original documents plus a summary; in the released code the walk only narrows the pool before a dense top-5, so the gap to the BGE baseline (also top-k dense) comes from which documents the walk reaches and from the summary.

In the code, a node with more than 3 unvisited neighbours makes the sampling call raise, and the walk falls back to plain retrieval; with semantic edges on, dense clusters make this common. The example script turns K-means off, leaving a pure temporal chain.
In Table 1 every LaMP-1 F1 is exactly half of the accuracy, and LaMP-2 F1 (0.025-0.031) is about a fifteenth of the accuracy; the paper does not explain these F1 values.
Without behavioral memory (summary only) LaMP-3 MAE is 0.64, worse than no personalization at all (0.52), so the summary alone hurts rating prediction.
Without edge weighting LaMP-1 accuracy (0.5708) is below the Random baseline (0.58).
The appendix memory baselines (Mem0, MemoRAG, Memory-R1, Table 5) come without setup details (backbone, what is stored), so how they were run cannot be checked.
Baselines' top-k is not stated in the paper; the code default is 5.
